Yes, Professor Margaret O. Sofidiya has conducted extensive research on the anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antioxidant activities of numerous other medicinal plants. [1, 2, 3] 
Her work primarily focuses on validating African traditional medicine through controlled laboratory and animal models. Some of the other notable plants she has evaluated for their anti-inflammatory properties include: [1, 4, 5, 6] 
## 1. Flabellaria paniculata

* Part Studied: Leaves
* Findings: In studies published by Sofidiya and her team, an ethanol extract of this plant demonstrated strong anti-inflammatory properties. It significantly suppressed tissue swelling across multiple chemical-induced animal models (carrageenan, serotonin, histamine, and xylene) and reduced critical pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-α. [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] 

## 2. [Margaritaria discoidea](https://www.google.com/search?q=margaritaria+discoidea&kgmid=/m/0c02d48#-wE)

* Part Studied: Stem bark
* Findings: Sofidiya's research investigated the aqueous extract of this plant, which is traditionally used to treat body pains. The study established that it substantially decreases paw edema (swelling) triggered by carrageenan and histamine, operating through mechanisms that mimic standard non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). [12, 13] 

## 3. Phaulopsis falcisepala

* Part Studied: Whole plant
* Findings: Her co-authored research evaluated the ethanol extract of this species in rodent models, validating its capabilities to interfere with early-phase and late-phase acute inflammatory pathways. [14] 

## 4. [Alafia barteri](https://www.google.com/search?q=alafia+barteri&kgmid=/m/0wy1qs_#-JmmDg), Combretum mucronatum, and Capparis thonningii

* Part Studied: Roots
* Findings: In a collaborative comparative study, Sofidiya investigated the methanol root extracts of these three traditional African medicinal plants. All three extracts (especially at 200 mg/kg doses) showed significant dual action—acting as both centralized pain-relievers (analgesics) and localized anti-inflammatory agents by inhibiting xylene- and carrageenan-induced edema. [4] 

## 5. [Malva parviflora](https://www.google.com/search?q=malva+parviflora&kgmid=/m/0479v1x#)

* Part Studied: Whole plant/leaves
* Findings: Sofidiya's research highlighted that the methanol extract of this plant contains a high concentration of total phenols and flavonoids, granting it strong free-radical scavenging abilities that directly correlate with its recorded anti-inflammatory and pain-reducing actions. [15, 16, 17, 18]
